title: Conduct and manage a multi-day horse trail

lessons.title: Planning a multi-day trail
lessons.html:
From day ride to expedition

A multi-day trail, such as a three-day ride through the Drakensberg foothills, the Karoo or along the Wild Coast, is a small expedition. Clients and horses are far from help for days, overnight in camps, huts or farmhouses. The trail manager carries overall responsibility for safety, welfare, logistics, legal compliance and the client experience, and leads a team of guides, grooms and support crew.

Route planning

  • Daily distances: plan realistic stages, typically about 20 to 35 km a day at mostly walking pace, depending on terrain, horse fitness and client ability. Reduce distances on steep or hot days.
  • Overnight stops: secure grazing or paddocks, clean water, shelter for horses and people, vehicle access for back-up.
  • Access and permissions: written agreements with landowners, communal authorities and conservation authorities for every section; know the rules on protected areas.
  • Hazards: river crossings (and how they change after rain), passes, fences, roads, wildlife, stock theft areas and lightning-prone ridges.
  • Escape routes: points along each day where an injured person or horse can be evacuated by vehicle; known nearest hospitals and vets.

Logistics

AreaPlanning items
HorsesFit, conditioned horses plus spares; feed, buckets, farrier kit, horse first aid, vet contact along the route
Back-up vehicleCarries luggage, food, water, horse feed, tack spares; horsebox for evacuation
Food and waterMenus, safe food storage, water purification
CommunicationCell coverage map, radios, satellite communicator where there is no signal; check-in schedule with base
StaffingGuide-to-client ratio, first aid-qualified staff, cook and grooms

Risk and legal compliance

Prepare a written risk assessment and emergency response plan. Check insurance (public liability), client indemnities, staff working hours and conditions under the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997, and health and safety duties under the OHS Act 85 of 1993. Horses moving between areas may need veterinary documents, including African horse sickness vaccination records and, where required, movement permits.

Budgeting

Cost every element per day in ZAR: horse feed and care, staff, food, accommodation and camp fees, vehicle fuel, insurance, landowner fees and contingency. Set a client price that covers costs, risk and margin.

lessons.title: Selecting clients and conditioning horses
lessons.html:
Selecting and preparing clients

Multi-day riding is physically demanding. Long hours in the saddle cause fatigue, saddle soreness and dehydration. Unsuitable clients put the whole group at risk.

  • State minimum requirements clearly in the marketing: e.g. able to rise to the trot and canter in control, ride for several hours on consecutive days, within a weight limit.
  • Screen clients with a questionnaire on experience, fitness, medical conditions, allergies and medication. Ask for a recent assessment ride if unsure.
  • Send a kit list: approved helmet, riding boots or boots with a heel, half-chaps, layers for cold mornings and hot afternoons, rain jacket, sunscreen, personal medication.
  • Hold a full briefing on arrival, covering safety rules, daily routine, camp etiquette, environmental rules and emergency procedures.
  • Do an assessment ride on day one before leaving the base, and adjust horse allocations.

Conditioning horses

Horses need a fitness programme of several weeks, building up distance, hills and consecutive days of work. A fit horse recovers its heart rate quickly after effort.

  • Check each horse's soundness, back and teeth before the trail.
  • Shoe a week or so before departure so any problems show early; carry spare shoes and a farrier kit or a trained person.
  • Saddles must fit each horse well; poorly fitted saddles cause back sores over consecutive days.
  • Match horse to rider: weight, experience and temperament.

Monitoring on the trail

CheckWhen
Heart rate recovery and breathingAfter climbs and at stops
Hydration (skin pinch, gums, drinking)Every stop
Back and girth area for heat or swellingAfter unsaddling, every evening
Legs and feet, shoesMorning and evening
Appetite and dungEvening and morning feed

Rest or swap any horse with back soreness, lameness, poor appetite or slow recovery. Record observations in a horse log for each day.

lessons.title: Running the trail and managing incidents
lessons.html:
The daily routine

  1. Early morning: check, water and feed horses; check feet and backs.
  2. Breakfast and briefing on the day's route, hazards, weather and stops.
  3. Tack up, check girths, mount and do a headcount.
  4. Ride in stages with rests every one to two hours; long lunch break in shade with horses unsaddled or girths loosened, watered and grazing.
  5. Arrive at camp with time to care for horses before dark: untack, wash or brush, check, water, feed and secure them in paddocks or on safe tethers.
  6. Evening debrief with staff; plan the next day; check in with base.

Managing people

  • Keep the pace to the least experienced rider; split the group into a slower and faster ride only if you have enough qualified guides.
  • Watch clients for fatigue, sunburn, dehydration and saddle sores; offer rest in the back-up vehicle.
  • Manage group dynamics: different expectations, alcohol at camp, early nights.
  • Respect communities and landowners; close gates, stay on agreed routes, and be courteous.

Environmental care

  • Leave no trace: carry out litter, use proper toilets or dig latrines well away from water.
  • Keep horses out of wetlands and off fragile slopes; avoid causing erosion on steep paths.
  • No open fires except where allowed, and never in high fire-danger weather.

Incident management

  • Injured rider: stop the ride, assess, give first aid, call 10177 or 112 or use a satellite communicator, and evacuate to the nearest vehicle access point.
  • Injured or lame horse: assess, treat with the horse first aid kit, lead to the next vehicle point, and arrange a vet or horsebox.
  • Lost rider or horse: stop the group, headcount, search systematically and alert base.
  • Weather: delay or reroute for storms, floods or extreme heat. A cancelled day is better than a disaster.

Record every incident with times, actions and witnesses, and report to management and insurers as required.

After the trail

Rest horses for several days, check them fully and treat any sores. Debrief staff, gather client feedback, reconcile the budget, and update the route plan and risk assessment.

Key points

  • Plan realistic stages, overnight stops, permissions and evacuation points.
  • Prepare a written risk assessment, emergency plan, insurance and budget.
  • Screen clients and condition horses over several weeks.
  • Check horses' backs, legs, hydration and appetite every day.
  • Leave no trace and respect landowners and communities.
  • Record and review every incident; rest horses after the trail.
